title: Study of the Influence of Quenching Cooling Medium and Tempering Temperature on the Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of DIN X20Cr13 Steel
abstract: Abstract DIN X20Cr13 martensitic stainless steel tubes are widely used in oil and gas services because they combine mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and microstructural stability. This study examines the effects of quenching media (still air and forced air, considering air and not merely a simple cooling medium) and tempering temperatures (600, 650, and 700 °C) on the mechanical behavior of this material. Tensile, impact, and Rockwell C hardness tests were carried out. Furthermore, the microstructures were characterized by x‑ray diffraction, optical microscopy, and scanning electron microscopy. The experimental data were analyzed using a full factorial design. The results indicated that forced‑air quenching favored the formation of a higher martensite fraction, which increased strength and produced a finer, more uniform structure. Tempering at 600 °C led to partial martensite breakdown and progressive carbide precipitation, causing hardness loss but improving toughness. Under the examined conditions, forced‑air quenching followed by tempering at 600 °C exhibited the highest yield strength of about 770-1020 MPa but the lowest impact toughness (≈ 7-20 J). In contrast, tempering at 650 °C provided the best strength–toughness balance for DIN X20Cr13 tubes in oil and gas service, achieving 734-835 MPa in yield strength and approximately 15-20 J in impact energy.
journal: Journal of Materials Engineering and Performance

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Martensitic stainless steels containing roughly 13% chromium are widely used in industrial applications that demand reliable hardening and strength after heat treatment. This is particularly relevant in oil and gas operations, where components such as valves and high-pressure piping rely on mechanical performance and resistance to harsh environments (Ref  1 ,  2 - 3 ).

When supplied in the hot-rolled condition, DIN X20Cr13 steel exhibits a ferritic matrix structure dotted with spheroidal M23C6 carbides, a typical feature of this processing route (Ref  4 ,  5 - 6 ). These initial microstructural attributes play a key role in determining how the steel reacts to subsequent heat treatments aimed at improving performance.

A common approach to enhancing the strength of this alloy involves austenitizing at approximately 1050 °C for an appropriate holding time, typically around 30 min. As the steel is held at this temperature, carbides dissolve, thereby creating a more uniform austenitic phase. The martensite created after controlled cooling is responsible for the hardness and high strength that make these steels so useful (Ref  7 ,  8 ). Mechanical parameters such as tensile strength, hardness, toughness, ductility, and corrosion resistance are strongly influenced by both the temperature selected and the cooling method used during quenching and tempering (Ref  9 ,  10 ).

Studies examining steels with compositions similar to X20Cr13 show that the choice of heat treatment parameters, including cooling medium and tempering temperature, affects the resulting microstructure, including the presence of carbides and retained austenite. These structural changes directly impact properties including toughness, corrosion resistance, and ductility. These studies have shown that microstructural shifts can result in notable variations in practical performance (Ref  9 ,  11 ,  12 ).

Investigating the influence of M 23 C 6  carbide content on the mechanical properties of AISI 420 steel, Bhadauria et al. (Ref  13 ) observed that carbide precipitation peaks occurred at 450 °C, enhancing the hardening of this material, whereas at higher tempering temperatures, carbide coarsening prevails and hardness decreases. Nevertheless, this behavior should be interpreted in the context of other structural changes during the tempering heat treatment. The ratio of martensite/retained austenite formed after quenching of AISI 420 steel can absorb mechanical energy due to strain-induced martensite transformation, thereby generating local hardening and lattice expansion that hinder crack propagation (Ref  14 ,  15 ).

The cooling rate is a decisive variable on the mechanical and microstructural responses of DIN X20Cr13 steel. In general, higher cooling rates reduce carbide precipitation at grain boundaries and retain more carbon in solid solution within the martensite lattice, leading to a finer martensite lath structure and, consequently, superior hardness and tensile resistance (Ref  11 ,  16 ,  17 ).

Although this knowledge is well established, there is no comprehensive and comparative discussion of air-based cooling regimes for DIN X20Cr13 steel. Published works often treat air cooling as a single condition, i.e., a simple quenching medium. Most studies do not consider variations in tempering temperature to achieve high strength and toughness for applications used in the oil and gas industries (Ref  18 ,  19 - 20 ).

Motivated by these aspects, the present work explores how varying the parameters involved in quenching and tempering, particularly the cooling medium (forced or still air) and tempering temperatures of 600, 650, and 700 °C, affects both mechanical behavior and the microstructural evolution of DIN X20Cr13 steel. This investigation aims to select the best practices for the heat treatment of components used in oil and gas industry applications, in line with current standards for quality and reliability.

sections.heading: Material and Heat Treatment
paragraphs: Specimens were obtained from a seamless tube of DIN X20Cr13 steel, typically used in the oil and gas industry, as shown in Fig.  1 . Tensile, Rockwell C hardness, impact, and microstructure analysis specimens were prepared in accordance with API SPEC 5CT (2023) and ISO 11960 (ISO, 2011) standards, as depicted in Fig.  2 . Chemical composition analysis was performed using inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry (ICP-OES), revealing the following composition: 0.20%C, 0.27%Si, 0.04%Mo, and 13.4%Cr (all in wt.%). The mechanical test specimens were extracted from the DIN X20Cr13 steel tube with an outer diameter of 200 mm and a wall thickness of 23 mm, Fig.  2 . Fig. 1 DIN X20Cr13 steel used as the source material for producing specimens designated for hardness measurements, optical microscopy, impact testing, and tensile tests Fig. 2 DIN X20Cr13 steel specimens prepared for: (a) tensile testing (HRC), (b) impact testing (OM), (c) optical microscopy, and (d) Rockwell hardness

Industrial heating furnaces (models TEMPER-T40 and TEMPER-R30) were used for the quenching and tempering heat treatments. These furnaces were calibrated to achieve the required austenitizing temperature for quenching and the specified temperatures for tempering. Three replicates were processed for each heat treatment condition listed in Table  1 . Table 1 Heat treatment conditions of DIN X20Cr13 Condition Austenitization Quenching cooling media Tempering temperature, °C Time, Minutes temperature, °C Time, Minutes Condition A 1050 30 Forced air 700 50 Condition B 1050 30 Still air 700 50 Condition C 1050 30 Forced air 650 50 Condition D 1050 30 Still air 650 50 Condition E 1050 30 Forced air 600 50 Condition F 1050 30 Still air 600 50

The selection of 1050 °C as the quenching temperature was intended to ensure sufficient dissolution of chromium-rich carbides (M 23 C 6 ) and to promote a stable austenitic structure while preventing excessive grain coarsening. While the selection of the austenitizing temperature was based on carbide dissolution, the tempering temperatures were chosen to systematically investigate the transition from a strength-dominated microstructure to one with higher toughness, which is essential for oil and gas applications (Ref  21 ).

Still-air cooling of the specimens was carried out on a bench at room temperature (20 ± 5 °C), whereas forced-air cooling was provided using a Makita® cordless blower (air volume: 13.4 m 3 /min; blowing force: 0-14.4 N). This procedure was adopted to ensure reproducibility and to minimize variability associated with air cooling. In this study, the effect of the cooling rate on the microstructure and mechanical behavior was comparatively examined, with all specimens austenitized under identical conditions and geometry and subjected to different cooling intensities for microstructural and mechanical analysis.

After the furnace reached the designated temperature, specimen temperature and soaking time were monitored using a calibrated Minipa MT-450A contact thermocouple to ensure accurate thermal treatment conditions, including appropriate temperature control, capacity, and volume for the heat treatment of steel test specimens, ensuring thermal stability and homogeneity in heating during the experimental stages.

sections.heading: Structural Analysis
paragraphs: Metallographic preparation involved sequential grinding with silicon carbide papers of various grit sizes, followed by polishing with diamond pastes of progressively finer particle sizes. Villela’s reagent was applied for three minutes to reveal microstructural features.

The initial microstructural examination was conducted using an Olympus BX60M optical microscope. Supplementary analysis of surface and phase features was performed using a JEOL JSM-7001F scanning electron microscope (SEM), employing two specimens per condition. Images were acquired from different regions of each specimen at three magnifications: 1000×, 2000×, and 10.000×. Phase identification employed x-ray diffraction (XRD technique), making use of a Shimadzu system equipped with a copper tube, operating in conventional Bragg–Brentano geometry. Detected peaks were compared with the PDF2 crystallographic database.

The carbide area fraction (%) was determined from SEM micrographs using an image binarization procedure (black–white thresholding in ImageJ), adapted from ASTM E1245 (2016). All images were acquired at the same magnification (10.000×). For each investigation, polishing artifacts, background noise, and non-microstructural features were excluded to avoid errors in determining the area content. The carbide area fraction was calculated as the ratio of the segmented carbide area to the total area of the analyzed image.

sections.heading: Mechanical Characterization and Statistical Analysis
paragraphs: Mechanical characterization included tensile tests performed on an Instron EMIC-23-1 M universal testing machine. Circular specimens (12.7 mm diameter) were extracted from the tube, with six specimens tested for each condition of DIN X20Cr13 steel. The crosshead speed was adjusted according to the testing stage. Nine Rockwell C hardness measurements were performed on the external surface, spaced 2.54-3.81 mm apart, using a Mitutoyo HR-400 durometer. A load of 10 kgf was applied, followed by a major load of 150 kgf, with a dwell time of 15 s. Impact toughness tests were conducted using an Instron MPX 750 J instrument. All mechanical tests were repeated at least three times to ensure reliability.

Mechanical property results, tensile parameters, Rockwell hardness, and impact energy were statistically investigated. Statistical analyses were employed to investigate the effects of quenching medium and tempering temperature on the mechanical properties of DIN X20Cr13 steel. Analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed using a full factorial design with two factors: quenching medium (two levels: still air and forced air) and tempering temperature (three levels: 600, 650, and 700 °C), adopting a 5% significance level. Sample sizes ranged from three to six specimens. The assumptions of normality and homogeneity of variance were assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk and Levene’s tests, respectively. The Student’s  t -distribution was used to estimate confidence intervals for the mean values of the mechanical properties. Statistical evaluation focused on main effects and interactions (Ref  23 ).

sections.heading: Mechanical Characterization
paragraphs: Austenitization was conducted at 1050 °C for half an hour. Forced air was used during cooling at a controlled rate, and this condition resulted in higher readings for yield strength, tensile strength, and hardness on the Rockwell scale (Ref  7 ). Examination of DIN X20Cr13 revealed clear effects of different cooling media and tempering conditions, as shown in Fig.  3  (yield strength) and Fig.  4  (all mechanical parameters of DIN X20Cr13 steel) and Table  2 , with all specimens austenitized at 1050 °C for 30 min. Fig. 3 Stress–strain engineering curves for still-air and forced-air cooling of DIN X20Cr13 steel for different tempering temperatures: (a) 600 °C, (b) 650 °C, (c) 700 °C Fig. 4 Mechanical properties of DIN X20Cr13 steel under different heat treatment conditions Table 2 Intervals for the mean mechanical properties of DIN X20Cr13 under different conditions (Student’s  t -distribution) Condition Yield strength, MPa Tensile strength, MPa Total elongation, % 600 °C still air 790.59 <  μ  < 841.41 990.59 <  μ  < 1041.41 2.59 <  μ  < 35.54 600 °C forced air 769.94 <  μ  < 1024.06 1053.17 <  μ  < 1082.61 16.43 <  μ  < 17.82 650 °C still air 704.32 <  μ  < 818.68 921.32 <  μ  < 1035.68 15.72 <  μ  < 16.79 650 °C forced air 734.17 <  μ  < 835.82 914.47 <  μ  < 1041.53 15.89 <  μ  < 18.03 700 °C still air 582.47 <  μ  < 709.53 804.03 <  μ  < 892.97 14.15 <  μ  < 26.85 700 °C forced air 603.32 <  μ  < 717.68 779.91 <  μ  < 945.09 18.35 <  μ  < 20.02

Testing revealed that specimens subjected to still-air cooling tended to have reduced mechanical strength and hardness. When the austenitizing treatment is performed properly, the existing M 23 C 6  carbides dissolve, allowing carbon to spread evenly throughout the austenite.

During cooling, martensite forms progressively as atomic mobility decreases. Slower cooling in still air allows greater atomic diffusion and, rather than promoting carbide dissolution, may lead to some precipitation or limited growth of M 23 C 6  carbides before the final microstructure is established. This results in martensite with a lower carbon content in solid solution, often leading to a slight reduction in hardness and strength compared to specimens quenched more abruptly under forced-air cooling (Ref  24 ).

Forced-air cooling has the opposite effect, maintaining a greater portion of martensite and higher carbon supersaturation as early precipitation is inhibited. When the steel is tempered at temperatures between 600 and 700 °C, strength and ductility depend not only on M 23 C 6  precipitation but also on how the structure reduces strength and recovers ductility. This can be seen in Fig.  4 , Table  2 , and Ref ( 25 ,  26 ), respectively.

Mechanical evaluation of DIN X20Cr13 steel revealed pronounced sensitivity for the cooling medium used during quenching and the tempering temperature. At 700 °C, substituting forced air for still air during quenching resulted in measurable differences: yield strength increased by 2.62%; tensile strength by 2.25%; and Rockwell hardness by 0.43% (Ref  27 ,  28 ).

The Rockwell hardness profile reflects the local mechanical response of the outer tube region where the indentations were performed, in accordance with API SPEC 5CT (2023). The highest hardness value, obtained at 600 °C, particularly under forced-air cooling, is consistent with the predominance of a martensitic matrix and, consequently, a lower degree of recovery. As the tempering temperature increased to 700 °C, hardness decreased due to recovery and decomposition of martensite, which progressively reduced matrix strengthening in DIN X20Cr13 steel, although carbide precipitation was detected at all tempering temperatures (Ref  29 ,  30 ).

Distinct mechanical behavior was observed at a tempering temperature of 650 °C. Modifying the cooling protocol from still air to forced air led to a 3.08% rise in yield strength, continued gains in tensile strength, and a 2.46% increase in Rockwell hardness. For specimens tempered at 600 °C, further increases were noted: 2.25% in yield strength; 1.65% in tensile strength; and 0.43% in hardness.

Forced-air cooling during quenching, together with tempering at the lowest temperature studied, produced the most substantial enhancement in mechanical strength among all conditions. The greater proportion of martensite and the reduced amount of retained austenite are considered decisive in generating increased hardness and strength under these circumstances (Ref  29 ,  30 ,  31 - 32 ).

Retention of the martensitic structure was more effective at lower tempering temperatures. Tempering at 600 °C resulted in higher martensite stability, reduced transformation, and the formation of fine, uniformly distributed carbides. This refined microstructure reflected positively on the material’s strength properties.

These results are consistent with those reported by Channa et al. (Ref  33 ), who showed that reducing the tempering temperature increases hardness in martensitic stainless steels, often at the expense of toughness and ductility. Pérez-Gonzalo et al. (Ref  31 ) reported that when martensite is preserved by low-temperature tempering, the observed trade-off is increased strength and hardness at the expense of ductility.

Figure  5  offers visual confirmation of these effects, with the greatest declines in absorbed energy and ductility, measured as total elongation, found in the specimens tempered at 600 and 650 °C. This variation aligns with known behavior for martensitic steels subjected to quenching and tempering: Greater martensite fraction boosts hardness, but the matrix exhibits less plasticity, which makes the alloy more brittle (Ref  9 ). Fig. 5 Ductility parameters under different heat treatment conditions

Fine, dispersed carbides, precipitated after quenching at low temperatures, serve as reinforcing agents and facilitate crack initiation. This dual effect is most pronounced at 650 and 600 °C, where a marked decline in energy absorption capacity and ductility is evident. The profile of DIN X20Cr13, as supported by the data in Fig.  5 , is defined by the characteristic balance between strength and toughness. The increase in strength associated with carbide precipitation is accompanied by reduced fracture resistance.

Table  3  summarizes the statistical outcomes of this study. Two process variables were examined: Factor A, the quenching medium (still air vs. forced air), and Factor B, the tempering temperature (600, 650, and 700 °C). All hypothesis tests used a 95% confidence level ( α  = 0.05). The results indicate that tempering temperature had the strongest effect on the responses. In particular, the 600 °C condition was influential for several measured properties.  F  tests (Fisher–Snedecor) consistently exceeded the critical values for Factor B, confirming its significance. See the numbers in bold in Table  3 .

Absorbed impact energy was the only property that did not show a statistically significant difference across the heat treatment conditions ( p  > 0.05). All other parameters exhibited significant effects, underscoring the dominant role of heat treatment variables in determining the alloy’s mechanical behavior.

These data indicate that tempering temperature is the primary factor governing the mechanical properties of DIN X20Cr13 steel, whereas the cooling medium acts as a secondary, yet still influential, variable affecting strength-related characteristics (Fig.  6 ). Fig. 6 Mechanical parameters of DIN X20Cr13 under different tempering temperature and cooling medium variables: (a) yield strength, (b) ultimate tensile strength

Impact energy showed less variation than the other mechanical parameters, indicating that this property was more sensitive to tempering temperature, as shown by the statistical analysis, which did not exhibit a significant effect of the cooling medium. This situation can be attributed to the fact that all investigated conditions retained a predominantly martensitic matrix after austenitization at 1050 °C; therefore, the sensitivity of the impact energy value depended on the competition between recovery/softening and carbide evolution during tempering. However, this limited change in impact energy should not be interpreted as an absence of microstructural changes, but rather as the result of competing mechanisms acting simultaneously during tempering.

sections.heading: Structural Characterization
paragraphs: Figure  7  compares the x-ray diffractograms of specimens quenched in forced air and in still air. With forced-air cooling, the diffraction lines appear noticeably broader, most clearly at the main reflection near 2 θ  ≈ 44.7°. This broadening is commonly attributed to the refinement of martensitic laths/packets, a higher dislocation content, and microstrain introduced during rapid heat extraction, as also discussed by Isakov et al. (Ref  34 ). Fig. 7 XRD diffractograms of the quenched specimens: (a) in still air and (b) in forced air

By contrast, the still-air condition exhibits narrower, well-defined peaks, indicative of grain coarsening and a reduced dislocation density, consistent with the slower cooling rate. A distinct feature near 2 θ  ≈ 44° may further indicate the presence of retained austenite, consistent with the behavior reported by Tavares et al. (Ref  35 ) under conditions that favor phase retention during slow cooling.

The micrographs in Fig.  8  and  9  indicate that martensite is the predominant phase in specimens cooled with forced air, consistent with the higher strength observed under this condition. Under still-air cooling, martensite is also present, but the resulting microstructure is generally associated with lower strength. The slower cooling rate, in turn, is compatible with improved dimensional stability and reduced residual stress (Ref  36 ). Fig. 8 SEM micrographs of DIN X20Cr13 steel processed by austenitization at 1050 °C for 30 min, followed by forced-air cooling, displayed across multiple magnification levels Fig. 9 SEM micrographs of DIN X20Cr13 steel processed by austenitization at 1050 °C for 30 min, followed by still-air cooling, displayed across multiple magnification levels

Figure  8  shows a fine, plate-like martensitic morphology, with narrow, similarly oriented plates. This refinement is typical of rapid cooling, which enlarges the number of nucleation events and limits subsequent coarsening. In Fig.  9 , representative of still-air cooling, the martensitic network is coarser and more needle-like, with thicker bundles; this appearance points to a less efficient transformation and may suggest a higher fraction of retained austenite (Ref  36 ,  37 ).

Figure  10  shows optical micrographs of the DIN X20Cr13 steel after quenching and tempering carried out under different conditions. It is important to note that all the specimens underwent austenitization at 1050 °C for 30 min before these treatments. The images make clear that tempering leads to carbide precipitation, while the matrix itself remains mostly martensitic. A closer look reveals that many of the particles are located at prior austenite grain boundaries and also within interdendritic regions. Their appearance is not uniform: Most of them display irregular shapes, and some are slightly elongated, which is typical of M 23 C 6  carbides, often reported in martensitic stainless steels (Ref  37 ,  38 ). Nevertheless, other carbide types may also be present at this stage. Fig. 10 Microstructures of DIN X20Cr13 steel after tempering, shown at different magnifications (OM) after austenitization at 1050 °C for 30 min followed by: (a) forced-air cooling + tempering at 700 °C for 50 min, (b) still-air cooling + tempering at 700 °C for 50 min, (c) forced-air cooling + tempering at 650 °C for 50 min, (d) still-air cooling + tempering at 650 °C for 50 min, (e) forced-air cooling + tempering at 600 °C for 50 min, (f) still-air cooling + tempering at 600 °C for 50 min

As optical microscopy does not allow a secure identification of phases, these observations must be treated as preliminary. Detailed confirmation will only be obtained through SEM examination combined with compositional analysis, which will also provide a clearer picture of how these carbides are distributed throughout the microstructure (Ref  37 ,  38 ). In this situation, across all tempering temperatures investigated in this work, EDS analysis revealed high contents of Cr (≅ 63.8%) and Fe (≅ 23.9%), with residual fractions of Mn, Mo, and V (Ref  39 ,  40 ).

Figure  11 ,  12 ,  13 ,  14 ,  15 , and  16  shows SEM images illustrating the microstructural changes. The influence of the quenching medium and tempering temperature becomes evident, enabling clearer identification of features in the tempered specimens. Fig. 11 SEM images of DIN X20Cr13 steel subjected to austenitization at 1050 °C for 30 min, forced-air quenching, and tempering at 700 °C for 50 min, presented at diverse magnification levels Fig. 12 SEM micrographs showing DIN X20Cr13 steel after austenitization at 1050 °C for 30 min, still-air cooling, and tempering at 700 °C for 50 min, captured at multiple magnifications Fig. 13 Microstructure of DIN X20Cr13 steel in the quenched and tempered condition: austenitized at 1050 °C for 30 min + forced-air cooling and tempered at 650 °C for 50 min, at different magnifications, SEM Fig. 14 SEM images illustrating the microstructure of DIN X20Cr13 steel following austenitization at 1050 °C for 30 min, subsequent still-air cooling, and tempering at 650 °C for 50 min, displayed at different magnifications Fig. 15 SEM micrographs of DIN X20Cr13 steel subjected to austenitization at 1050 °C for 30 min, forced-air cooling, and tempering at 600 °C for 50 min, presented across different magnifications Fig. 16 SEM images displaying the microstructure of DIN X20Cr13 steel after austenitization at 1050 °C for 30 min, still-air cooling, and tempering at 600 °C for 50 min, shown at multiple magnification levels

Figure  11  and  12  illustrate the microstructural differences found in the DIN X20Cr13 steel tempered at 700 °C. In the specimen cooled with forced air (Fig.  12 ), the structure appears more uniform, with secondary carbides distributed in a fine and relatively regular manner. By contrast, the specimen cooled in still air (Fig.  11 ) exhibits a coarser morphology, with martensite packets and carbides showing greater irregularity and heterogeneity.

These variations in carbide morphology can be explained by diffusion mechanisms operating during tempering at 700 °C. The slower cooling rate in still air provides more time for atomic diffusion, which encourages carbide growth and coalescence. On the other hand, forced air restricts this movement, leading to smaller carbides that remain evenly dispersed in the matrix (Ref  41 ,  42 ).

A similar situation occurs at 650 °C, as shown in Fig.  13  and  14 . Once again, forced-air cooling produces finer and more homogeneous carbide distributions, while specimens cooled in still air develop a comparatively coarser arrangement within the martensitic matrix (Ref  18 ,  19 - 20 ).

In Fig.  13  and  14 , micrographs of specimens tempered at 650 °C illustrate the influence of the cooling method on the final microstructure. When forced-air cooling is applied after quenching (Fig.  13 ), the tempered martensite appears finer, and secondary carbides are more uniformly and stably distributed. In contrast, specimens cooled in still air (Fig.  14 ) exhibit a coarser microstructure, with both martensite and carbides appearing more pronounced, as well as a greater presence of coalesced particles that are larger and more widely spaced.

Carbide location also varies. In the forced-air specimen, precipitates tend to align along martensite boundaries, often in a regular pattern. Under still-air cooling, carbides are distributed less uniformly, indicating that the slower cooling rate enhances diffusion and promotes coarsening through coalescence. The set of images is completed by Fig.  15  and  16 , which show the microstructure for specimens tempered at 600 °C, comparing forced-air and still-air cooling once again.

Considering Fig.  15  and  16 , significant differences between cooling routes become immediately apparent for specimens tempered at 600 °C. In Fig.  15 , forced-air cooling produces tempered martensite with a notably fine microstructure, in which the carbides remain small and evenly spaced throughout the metallic matrix. In the case of still-air cooling (Fig.  16 ), the outcome diverges: Martensite domains appear bulkier, and carbides are enlarged, sometimes forming isolated clusters. This pattern stems from the greater atomic mobility permitted by slower cooling, which enables both the enlargement and merging of precipitate particles before the structure stabilizes (Ref  43 ).

These findings confirm that cooling intensity and tempering temperature interact to define the microstructure, as shown in Fig.  17 , which presents the evolution of carbide area fraction across all heat treatment conditions. Based on Fig.  17  and Fig.  8 ,  9 ,  10 ,  11 ,  12 ,  13 ,  14 ,  15 , and  16 , carbide precipitation is strongly influenced by both the quenching medium and the tempering temperature. In general, specimens cooled in still air and tempered at 600 and 650 °C exhibited higher carbide fractions, whereas tempering at 700 °C resulted in the lowest carbide fraction among the temperatures investigated. Fig. 17 Carbides fraction (%) for different heat treatment conditions of the DIN X20Cr13 steel

These results suggest that the thermal path modified the amount, morphology, coalescence, and distribution of carbides. Still-air cooling promotes coarser and more heterogeneous carbide arrangements, whereas forced-air cooling leads to a finer and more uniform carbide distribution.

Specimens subjected to rapid cooling by forced air exhibit elongated, well-aligned martensitic regions, accompanied by finer carbides that are more uniformly dispersed. These microstructural features are typically associated with enhanced mechanical strength. In contrast, the microstructure after still-air cooling is less organized and marked by coarser martensite and more pronounced carbide aggregation, typical of increased diffusion during the transformation. Higher tempering temperatures further amplify these contrasts, driving greater precipitation, hastening the reduction of martensite content, and thus reducing the mechanical strength.

The evolution of the mechanical properties of the DIN X20Cr13 steel, as reflected in the yield strength, tensile strength, and Rockwell hardness values shown in Fig.  3 , is associated with the combined influence of martensite content, as well as the morphology and quantity of carbide precipitation. All heat-treated conditions exhibited an area fraction of Cr-rich M 23 C 6  carbides, whereas the matrix remained predominantly martensitic. Forced-air quenching produces a finer and more homogeneous martensitic structure compared to still-air cooling, while also promoting the formation of smaller, more uniformly dispersed carbides. In contrast, cooling in still air promotes carbide growth and partial coalescence, resulting in a coarser and more heterogeneous carbide morphology.

The results from different techniques showed that mechanical strength is not governed by carbide fraction alone. Tempering at 600 °C under forced-air conditions exhibited the highest yield and tensile strengths and Rockwell hardness values, despite not having the highest carbide fraction. It indicates that the dominant strengthening mechanism in this situation is better explained by the persistence of a refined, tempered martensitic matrix and reduced recovery. In contrast, the progressive increase in the tempering temperature is accompanied by homogeneous growth in the Scherrer-based apparent crystallite size, indicating reduced peak broadening, lower lattice distortion, and decreased strengthening contribution from the matrix as shown in Table  4 . This result suggests that the increase in the apparent crystallite size observed by XRD reflects softening of the tempered martensitic matrix rather than mechanical strengthening (Ref  44 ). Table 4 Apparent crystallite size of martensite with tempering temperature and cooling medium variables Condition Apparent crystallite size of martensite, nm Quenching 1050 °C/still air 17.1 ± 3.0 Quenching 1050 °C/forced air 15.1 ± 3.8 Tempering 600 °C/still air 24.4 ± 5.5 Tempering 600 °C/forced air 26.1 ± 4.8 Tempering 650 °C/still air 26.7 ± 4.5 Tempering 650 °C/forced air 24.2 ± 5.4 Tempering 700 °C/still air 26.5 ± 4.3 Tempering 700 °C/forced air 27.0 ± 4.9

For a structural overview, Fig.  18  provides x-ray diffractograms of the alloy following variations in both cooling and tempering. Notable diffraction maxima occur at 44.7°, 65.0°, and 82.3° (2 θ ), corresponding to the (110), (200), and (211) planes. These reflections are indicative of the  α ′or  α -Fe phase—either the slightly deformed body-centered tetragonal lattice of martensite or the ideal body-centered cubic ferrite. Although these two phases differ structurally, their diffractograms overlap at these positions, allowing both to be identified by examination of these characteristic signals (Ref  45 ,  46 - 47 ). Fig. 18 XRD diffractogram of DIN X20Cr13 steel, tempered at different temperatures and cooling media: forced air and still air

The  α ′-Fe phase ( α ′) appeared in every diffractogram, while the shape and strength of the peaks changed depending on the tempering conditions. At 700 °C, the peaks were less sharp and their heights decreased compared to lower temperatures, suggesting deeper martensite transformation and more advanced carbide formation, with particles tending toward a rounded contour as precipitation increased. For specimens tempered at 650 °C with forced air, similar changes were observed, but the degree of martensite breakdown was less marked than at the higher temperature, which was beneficial to the toughness of DIN X20Cr13 steel.

In still air, the steel tempered at 600 °C exhibits a noticeably altered microstructure, with martensite forming very fine, consistent laths. This indicates a more stable lath network and promotes both the breakdown of martensite and the development of ferrite. The corresponding diffractograms made this clear, showing dense arrangements of martensite packets and interfaces located close together, features that signal an elevated amount of martensite remaining in the steel after tempering.

The mechanical and structural results demonstrated that the mechanical behavior of DIN X20Cr13 steel depends on the cooling rate used during austenitization. Studying carbide evolution and martensite arrangement across all heat treatments is a requirement to expand the applications of this steel in the oil and gas industry.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This study evaluated the most effective quenching and tempering conditions for DIN X20Cr13 steel for applications where mechanical strength and wear resistance are essential, such as the oil and gas industry. The main conclusions reached in this work are described: The mechanical behavior of DIN X20Cr13 was determined by the combined effect of quenching, cooling intensity, and tempering temperature. Forced air produced a noticeably finer martensitic structure, with carbides distributed more regularly in the matrix, beneficial for strength. Still air resulted in coarser martensite and more heterogeneous carbides, generally leading to lower strength and hardness than forced-air cooling. The increase in tempering temperature from 600 to 700 °C accelerated martensite recovery and carbide coarsening, reducing mechanical strength. Among the investigated conditions, tempering at 650 °C provided the most favorable balance between strength and toughness for the application of DIN X20Cr13 steel tubes in oil and gas services.
